hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? what’s one chore you’d happily never do again?
options: classic. this story might change how they feel.
fair. you’re about to meet a man with buckets.

steps.line: Cleanthes was a boxer who came to Athens, the story goes, with almost no money. He wanted to study with Zeno at the painted porch.
So every night he drew water from the wells in the city’s gardens, bucket after bucket. By day, he studied.

steps.q: People wonder how he lives without seeming to work. He’s called before the court. Who does he bring?
o: A rich friend who paid his way
The people he worked for at night
steps.why: Witnesses to his night work. Honest proof.

steps.line: Summoned to explain how he lived, he brought witnesses: the gardener whose water he drew, and a woman whose grain he ground.

steps.q: The court is so impressed it votes him a gift of money. What does Zeno tell him?
steps.why: Turn it down. Diogenes Laertius puts the gift at ten minae, a real sum for a man drawing water at night.

steps.line: The court was so impressed it voted him a gift of money. Zeno told him not to accept it.

steps.q: Why might Zeno tell him to refuse the money?
o: His own work was already enough
A gift would leave him owing the city
The court was trying to trick him
steps.why: The water carrying wasn’t a problem to be solved. It was part of who he was becoming.

steps.line: Other students called him the donkey. Fine, he said: then I’m the one strong enough to carry Zeno’s load. He wrote his notes on oyster shells.

steps.pre: Zeno compared Cleanthes to a hard wax tablet: tough to write on, but it
steps.why: Diogenes Laertius records it. Quick minds take an impression fast; Cleanthes was slow, but what went in stayed.

steps.line: When Zeno died, the one who took over the school wasn’t the quickest student. It was Cleanthes, the water carrier.
Today: the dishes at ten at night. One plate, then the next. Not beneath you. Carry the water.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Stoics split life into what’s up to us and what isn’t. Which was up to Cleanthes?
steps.why: Epictetus, a later Stoic, built his teaching on that line. Cleanthes couldn’t choose the nickname, only what he did with it.

say: here’s what i love. the slow student, the one they called the donkey, ended up leading the school. no task was beneath him.

the stoics taught that humble work and high work are done by the same character. drawing water well and studying well are one practice. that’s this week: an emperor, an enslaved teacher, a shipwrecked merchant, a cynic, and a boxer with a bucket.

steps.q: When Zeno died, the school went to Cleanthes, not a quicker student. What does that suggest the Stoics valued most?
o: Strength, since he’d been a boxer
steps.why: His philosophy wasn’t only on the porch. It was at the well too, bucket after bucket.

today.say: today, pick one humble task, the dishes, the trash, a boring email, and do it slowly and well, like cleanthes drawing water. one bucket, then the next. notice how it changes when it isn’t beneath you.

card.keepWhy: No task is beneath you when it’s done well.
sources: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.168–176: Cleanthes of Assos, first a boxer; came to Athens with four drachmas; drew water by night in gardens and studied by day; called the Well-drawer; summoned before the court (the Areopagus) to explain how he lived, he brought the gardener whose water he drew and the woman whose meal he ground; the court voted him ten minas, which Zeno would not let him accept; called an ass by fellow students, he said he alone could bear Zeno’s burden; wrote on oyster shells and the shoulder-blades of oxen because he could not buy paper; succeeded Zeno as head of the school.
